power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps < 0.05", Text = "Post-hoc comparisons showed that animations with relatively low cross-avatar consistency (AU6, AU7, AU17, AU23) differed significantly from those with very high consistency (AU1, AU2, AU10, AU12, browsAU10; all ps < 0.05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .17", "p = .508", "p = .43", "p = .316", "p = .98", "p = 0.162"), Sentence = c("Overall AUC did not differ significantly between OF (M = 0.71, SD = 0.19) and AFAR (M = 0.67, SD = 0.21; This can be because the effect size is not clearly labeled (e.g., d, instead of d_rm), because the effect sizes is not reported with enough precisions (e.g., 0.3 instead of 0.32), or because the effect size is incorrectly reported.

table.text: Across systems, performance was significantly above chance (M = 0.69, SD = 0.20; t(143) = 11.3, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.94).

table.eta_coherence_note: Eta-squared reported; cannot be reconstructed from F and dfs in factorial or repeated-measures designs.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 79 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

5 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook files bundle the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the files itself, with nothing re-run. info.title: Benchmarking and Quantifying Facial Motion With Controlled Photorealistic Avatars

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								Justus Liebig University
								
									Giessen

Department of Computer Science
								Justus Liebig University
								
									Giessen

Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior
								Universities of Marburg
								
									Giessen
									and Darmstadt

text.text: Facial expressions are central to human social interaction, yet reliably quantifying how faces move over time remains challenging.
Here, we address these limitations in three ways.
First, we leverage photorealistic MetaHuman animations with precisely specified facial motion to systematically evaluate two widely used AU detection systems: AFAR and OpenFace.
Four avatars were animated with identical motion parameters to generate 72 videos comprising single-AU and AU-combination sequences.
Although both systems performed above chance, their performance varied substantially across AUs and avatars.

Second, we introduce and validate a complementary landmark-displacement approach that directly quantifies nonrigid facial motion from tracked geometry, yielding consistent and robust motion estimates across avatars and animations.
Third, we provide FACET, an open-source toolbox that integrates AU detection and landmark-based motion analysis within a unified and reproducible framework.

Together, our findings reveal systematic biases in current AU-detection systems, highlight the potential of landmark-based analysis to characterize facial motion directly, and provide an open, reproducible framework for quantifying facial motion and evaluating the methods used to capture it.
Facial expressions are vital for human communication and social interaction, allowing observers to infer others' emotions, intentions and mental states.
Although faces are inherently dynamic, much of face perception research has relied on static images (Dawel et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Although faces are inherently dynamic, much of face perception research has relied on static images <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dawel et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, psychophysical and neuroimaging evidence consistently shows that facial motion provides important information for face perception (Krumhuber et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Yet, psychophysical and neuroimaging evidence consistently shows that facial motion provides important information for face perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Krumhuber et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The human visual system is highly sensitive to the precise dynamics of facial motion (Dobs et al., 2014), and dynamic compared with static stimuli can enhance face and expression recognition, particularly when expressions are subtle or ambiguous (Richoz et al., 2024; Yovel & O'Toole, 2016).
text.formatted: The human visual system is highly sensitive to the precise dynamics of facial motion <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dobs et al., 2014)</ref>, and dynamic compared with static stimuli can enhance face and expression recognition, particularly when expressions are subtle or ambiguous <ref type="bibr">(Richoz et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Yovel & O'Toole, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Neuroimaging studies further suggest partly distinct neural mechanisms for processing dynamic and static faces (Bernstein & Yovel, 2015; Duchaine & Yovel, 2015; Pitcher et al., 2014; Pitcher & Ungerleider, 2021; Prabhakar et al., 2026; Puce, 2024).
text.formatted: Neuroimaging studies further suggest partly distinct neural mechanisms for processing dynamic and static faces <ref type="bibr">(Bernstein & Yovel, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Duchaine & Yovel, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pitcher et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pitcher & Ungerleider, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Prabhakar et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Puce, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings highlight the importance of facial motion for understanding face perception.

However, studying facial motion requires methods that allow researchers not only to generate naturalistic yet experimentally controlled dynamic face stimuli, but also to reliably quantify how faces move over time.
A variety of approaches have been used to create dynamic face stimuli, each involving different trade-offs between naturalism and experimental control (Dobs et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A variety of approaches have been used to create dynamic face stimuli, each involving different trade-offs between naturalism and experimental control <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dobs et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Real face videos offer high ecological validity but provide limited control over facial motion parameters (Dawel et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Real face videos offer high ecological validity but provide limited control over facial motion parameters <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dawel et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Wang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, 3D computer-generated (CG) faces afford fine-grained parametrization (Egger et al., 2020; Grewe et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2025), but may appear less natural or evoke uncanny responses (Crookes et al., 2015; Di Natale et al., 2023; Vaitonytė et al., 2023), and can produce altered behavioral and neural responses compared with real faces (Kätsyri et al., 2020; Kegel et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Conversely, 3D computer-generated (CG) faces afford fine-grained parametrization <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Egger et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Grewe et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Wu et al., 2025)</ref>, but may appear less natural or evoke uncanny responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crookes et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Di Natale et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Vaitonytė et al., 2023)</ref>, and can produce altered behavioral and neural responses compared with real faces <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Kätsyri et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Kegel et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Miller et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these limitations diminish with increasing photorealism: both perceived eeriness and neural differences relative to real faces are reduced for highly realistic CG stimuli (Higgins et al., 2021; Nasser Oesterreich et al., 2025; Schindler et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Importantly, these limitations diminish with increasing photorealism: both perceived eeriness and neural differences relative to real faces are reduced for highly realistic CG stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Higgins et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Nasser Oesterreich et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Schindler et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Recent advances in graphics technology may therefore help overcome the traditional trade-off between naturalism and experimental control when generating dynamic face stimuli.

One such platform is Unreal Engine's MetaHuman (MH) framework (Epic Games, 2019), which provides freely accessible photorealistic avatars with detailed facial rigs that enable precise control over anatomically plausible facial motion (Giuliana, 2022).
text.formatted: One such platform is Unreal Engine's MetaHuman (MH) framework (Epic Games, 2019), which provides freely accessible photorealistic avatars with detailed facial rigs that enable precise control over anatomically plausible facial motion <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Giuliana, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: MH avatars have recently been adopted across media, education, and experimental psychology (Bae et al., 2025; Haddick et al., 2022).
text.formatted: MH avatars have recently been adopted across media, education, and experimental psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bae et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Haddick et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Comparative work shows that MH stimuli appear more humanlike than other digital human systems (Bae et al., 2025) and can reduce the uncanny valley effects commonly associated with CG faces (Fraser et al., 2024; Haddick et al., 2022; Mori et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Comparative work shows that MH stimuli appear more humanlike than other digital human systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bae et al., 2025)</ref> and can reduce the uncanny valley effects commonly associated with CG faces <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fraser et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Haddick et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mori et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Recent datasets further demonstrate that MH avatars are perceived as realistic, friendly, and likable across diverse samples (Tsenkova et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent datasets further demonstrate that MH avatars are perceived as realistic, friendly, and likable across diverse samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Tsenkova et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Critically, their rig-based parametrization allows facial motion to be precisely specified across time and reproduced across different identities.
This combination of photorealism and experimental control makes MH avatars particularly well suited for generating dynamic facial stimuli with known underlying motion.

To quantify facial motion in dynamic stimuli, researchers commonly rely on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) (Ekman et al., 2002), an anatomically grounded framework that decomposes facial expressions into individual Action Units (AUs) defined by the underlying musculature (Zhi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: To quantify facial motion in dynamic stimuli, researchers commonly rely on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) <ref type="bibr">(Ekman et al., 2002)</ref>, an anatomically grounded framework that decomposes facial expressions into individual Action Units (AUs) defined by the underlying musculature <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Zhi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a smile involves contraction of the zygomatic major muscle, which pulls up the lip corners (AU12), often accompanied by activation of the outer portion of the orbicularis oculi, which raises the cheeks (AU6).
Manual FACS coding, however, is highly labor-intensive, requiring extensive training and frame-wise annotation of video sequences (Girard & Cohn, 2016; Stöckli et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Manual FACS coding, however, is highly labor-intensive, requiring extensive training and frame-wise annotation of video sequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Girard & Cohn, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Stöckli et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, automated AU detection systems such as OpenFace (Baltrusaitis et al., 2016) and the AFAR toolbox (Ertugrul et al., 2019a) are increasingly used to quantify facial behavior.
text.formatted: As a result, automated AU detection systems such as OpenFace <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baltrusaitis et al., 2016)</ref> and the AFAR toolbox <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Ertugrul et al., 2019a)</ref> are increasingly used to quantify facial behavior.

text.text: Despite their widespread adoption in psychological and behavioral research (Ambrosen et al., 2025; Darzi et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2018; Hickman et al., 2022; Hirsch et al., 2023; Namba et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023), the performance and potential biases of these systems remain insufficiently understood (Ertugrul et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2023; Namba et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Despite their widespread adoption in psychological and behavioral research <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ambrosen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Darzi et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Guo et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hickman et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hirsch et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Namba et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Zhao et al., 2023)</ref>, the performance and potential biases of these systems remain insufficiently understood <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Ertugrul et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kim et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Namba et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Characterizing such biases is particularly difficult using naturalistic video datasets, in which the underlying facial motion is not precisely known.

Controlled dynamic stimuli with known motion parameters therefore provide an important opportunity to systematically evaluate automated AU detection and determine how reliably these systems capture the specified facial motion.
Complementary to AU-based approaches, facial motion can be quantified more directly from changes in facial geometry.

Landmark-based approaches track the positions of anatomically defined facial points across time and characterize motion through changes in their positions, distances, or spatial configurations (Ko, 2018; Rajan et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Landmark-based approaches track the positions of anatomically defined facial points across time and characterize motion through changes in their positions, distances, or spatial configurations <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Ko, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Rajan et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Such approaches have been used, for example, to distinguish spontaneous from posed smiles and more broadly to characterize facial expressions for automatic emotion recognition (Park et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Such approaches have been used, for example, to distinguish spontaneous from posed smiles and more broadly to characterize facial expressions for automatic emotion recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Park et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Yan et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike AU detection, these approaches do not require observed facial motion to be classified into predefined action categories, providing a complementary description of where and how much the face moves.
However, the extent to which landmark-based measures reliably capture known facial motion across different identities and types of facial movement remains unclear.
Here, we use controlled facial animations in which motion parameters are precisely specified and reproduced across photorealistic MH avatars to achieve three aims.
First, we systematically evaluate the performance and potential biases of widely used automated AU detection systems.
Second, we develop and evaluate a complementary landmark-displacement approach that directly quantifies facial motion from tracked geometry.

Third, we introduce the open-source Facial Analysis, Coding and Evaluation Toolbox (FACET), which integrates automated AU detection and landmark-based motion analysis within a unified and reproducible framework for applying and systematically benchmarking facial motion quantification methods.

To systematically evaluate methods for quantifying facial motion, we created controlled facial animations with precisely specified motion parameters using the MetaHuman (MH) plugin (MetaHuman Creator, 2022) in Unreal Engine 5 (UE5) (Unreal Engine 5, 2022), an advanced 3D graphics engine.
Four freely available MH avatars were selected from the plugin's library (two male, two female; estimated ages 20-50 years; Figure 1A).
text.formatted: Four freely available MH avatars were selected from the plugin's library (two male, two female; estimated ages 20-50 years; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: Animations were generated in Python 3.10.6 using the UE5 Python API, which provides programmatic access to the facial rig system.
The UE5 facial rig is based on FACS (Ekman et al., 2002), allowing frame-by-frame manipulation of individual AUs through continuous activation parameters ranging from 0 to 1.
text.formatted: The UE5 facial rig is based on FACS <ref type="bibr">(Ekman et al., 2002)</ref>, allowing frame-by-frame manipulation of individual AUs through continuous activation parameters ranging from 0 to 1.

text.text: This enabled precise control over AU onset, peak, and offset timing.
These resulting frame-wise AU activation trajectories served as the ground truth for subsequent evaluation of the facial motion quantification methods.

Critically, identical motion parameters were applied to all four avatars, allowing us to assess the consistency of facial motion estimates across different faces while holding the underlying animation parameters constant.
For each avatar, we created 18 animations, yielding 72 animations in total.
Animations were of two types: single-AU animations (n=11) and AU-combination animations (n=7) (Table 1).

text.text: Single-AU animations allowed us to evaluate individual facial movements in isolation, whereas AU-combination animations provided more complex patterns of co-occurring facial motion.
Each animation comprised 60 frames and began with a neutral face.

text.text: As a complementary approach to AU-based motion quantification, we developed a pipeline that directly characterizes facial motion from landmark displacements (Figure 4A).
text.formatted: As a complementary approach to AU-based motion quantification, we developed a pipeline that directly characterizes facial motion from landmark displacements (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4A</ref>).

text.text: We used OF's facial landmark extraction module, which provides 3D coordinates for 51 within-face landmarks alongside the AU predictions.

Although the present animations were rendered from a fixed frontal viewpoint with minimal rigid motion, we implemented a rigidmotion correction procedure to facilitate application of the pipeline to videos containing head movement.

Using OF's frame-wise estimates of 3D translation (x,y,z) and head rotation (roll, pitch, yaw), translation vectors were first subtracted from the raw landmark coordinates, after which the inverse rotation matrix for each frame was applied to remove rigid head-motion components (facet.au_detection.landmarks.inverse_affine_transform).
The resulting coordinates were then mean-centered across landmarks to remove residual global positional offsets.

Facial motion was quantified as the Euclidean distance between the corrected 3D position of each landmark at each frame and its position in the initial neutral frame, yielding a 51 x 60 landmark-displacement matrix for each animation.
Because displacement was calculated relative to each avatar's own neutral configuration, static differences in facial geometry across avatars did not directly contribute to the displacement measure.
Displacement values therefore represent the magnitude of nonrigid landmark movement in 3D space relative to the neutral configuration.
We characterized the resulting displacement profiles using two complementary analyses.

First, to assess the consistency of facial motion across avatars, we computed pairwise correlations (Pearson's r) between the displacement matrices of different avatars for each animation (facet.au_detection.displacement_analysis.compute_pairwise_displacement_ correlations).

We summarized these correlations both across animations for each avatar pair, to assess overall consistency across faces, and across avatar pairs for each animation, to determine whether cross-avatar consistency varied across facial movements.

Then, to evaluate whether displacement was spatially concentrated in facial regions expected to move for a given AU, we calculated the ratio between the mean displacement of AU-relevant landmarks and the mean displacement of all remaining landmarks (facet.au_detection.displacement_analysis.compute_expected_motion_ratio).
For example, for an AU1 animation, the expected-to-be-active set comprised eyebrow landmarks.

Methods for quantifying facial motion are implemented across different software environments, rely on distinct dependencies, and vary in their input requirements, processing interfaces, and output structures.
These differences can make it cumbersome to process larger datasets, combine multiple methods within a single analysis pipeline, and compare their outputs in a standardized manner.

To address these challenges, we developed the Facial Analysis, Coding and Evaluation Toolbox (FACET), an open-source Python toolbox that provides a unified framework for applying and systematically benchmarking facial motion quantification methods.
FACET integrates automated AU detection and landmark-based motion analysis within a consistent application programming interface (API).

It provides standardized input handling and batch processing of multiple files, allowing users to run supported AU detectors, quantify facial motion from landmark displacement, and generate corresponding visualizations within a common workflow.

FACET can additionally convert detector-specific outputs into a standardized BIDS-like format, allowing downstream analyses to operate on a common data structure irrespective of the original detector or output format (e.g., .mat or .npy).
FACET can be installed as a Python package or run within a Docker container, facilitating reproducible use across computing environments.

The analyses reported in the present study were originally conducted using the individual software environments described above, reflecting heterogeneous workflows currently required to combine different facial analysis tools.
FACET integrates these analysis steps within a common framework, and we provide the corresponding FACET functions alongside each analysis below.

This allows researchers to reproduce the present analyses, apply individual components to their own data, and use controlled stimuli with known motion parameters to benchmark facial motion quantification methods.

To examine how well each AU detection system captured the temporal dynamics of AU activation, we quantified the correspondence between predicted AU time series and the ground-truth activation trajectories specified by the facial rig in UE5.
For each AU and animation, predicted and ground-truth time series were z-normalized, and their crosscorrelation was calculated at zero lag.

At zero lag, the normalized cross-correlation is equivalent to the Pearson correlation coefficient (r), with higher values indicating greater similarity in the temporal profile of predicted and ground-truth AU activation across frames.
This measure therefore captures temporal alignment in the shape of the activation trajectories rather than agreement in their absolute magnitude.
FACET additionally supports lagged crosscorrelation and further analyses of temporal dynamics through its au_detection.temporal module.

However, given the small number of avatars (two male, two female), these differences cannot be attributed specifically to avatar sex and may reflect other differences in facial form or appearance.
Both TPR and FPR varied substantially across animations (TPR: χ²(17) = 44.8, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.66; FPR: χ²(17) = 51.51, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.76; Figure 2C).

text.text: Animations of AU7 (lid tightener), AU12 (lip corner puller) and AU14 (dimpler) yielded the highest TPRs, whereas AU6 (cheek raiser), AU2 (outer brow raiser) and AU17 (chin raiser) yielded the lowest.
FPRs also varied systematically across facial movements.

Several animations involving smiling-related movements, particularly browsAU12, AU12, and browsAU10, produced high FPRs, whereas AU4 (brow lowerer), AU23 (lip tightener) and browsAll showed comparatively low FPRs.
The combination of high TPR and elevated FPR for smile-related movements (especially AU12, lip corner puller) suggests an increased tendency of the systems to predict smile-related AUs.
Overall, OF and AFAR showed moderate classification performance, with substantial variation across facial movements and avatars.
Although average AUC did not differ across avatars, threshold-based analyses revealed systematic avatar-dependent differences in both true-and false-positive rates.
Classification performance also varied strongly across AUs, with high performance for some facial movements but poor discrimination or elevated false-positive rates for others.

Together, these findings show that automated AU detection does not capture different facial movements and faces equally reliably, even when the underlying AU activation trajectories are precisely controlled.

To quantify facial motion independently of the AU prediction step, we computed displacement across 51 within-face landmarks for all 72 animations (Figure 4A).
text.formatted: To quantify facial motion independently of the AU prediction step, we computed displacement across 51 within-face landmarks for all 72 animations (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4A</ref>).

text.text: Landmark positions were obtained using OF's facial landmark tracker, but the subsequent analyses did not rely on its AU predictions.
Because identical facial rigging parameters were applied across avatars, a consistent motion descriptor should yield similar displacement patterns across avatars for the same animation.
Overall, cross-avatar consistency was high, with a mean pairwise correlation of r = 0.87 (SD = 0.13) across animations.
Moreover, mean correlations exceeded .80 for every avatar pair (Figure 4B), indicating that landmark displacement yielded highly consistent estimates of facial motion across the four avatars.
text.formatted: Moreover, mean correlations exceeded .80 for every avatar pair (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4B</ref>), indicating that landmark displacement yielded highly consistent estimates of facial motion across the four avatars.

text.text: Next, we examined whether cross-avatar consistency varied across facial movements (Figure 4C).
text.formatted: Next, we examined whether cross-avatar consistency varied across facial movements (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4C</ref>).

text.text: With the exception of AU7 (lid tightener), all animations showed mean crossavatar correlations above 0.70.

The highest consistency was observed for AU12 (lip corner puller; M = 0.98, SD = 0.01), browsAU10 (M = 0.98, SD = 0.01), AU2 (outer brow raiser; M = 0.97, SD = 0.02), AU1 (inner brow raiser; M = 0.96, SD = 0.01), AU10 (upper lip raiser; M = 0.95, SD = 0.01), and AU14 (dimpler; M = 0.95, SD = 0.03).
The lowest consistency was observed for AU7 (lid tightener; M = 0.57, SD = 0.22), AU17 (chin raiser; M = 0.72, SD = 0.18), and AU6 (cheek raiser; M = 0.73, SD = 0.08).
Cross-avatar consistency differed significantly across animations (χ 2 (17) = 94.409, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.93).

text.text: Post-hoc comparisons showed that animations with relatively low cross-avatar consistency (AU6, AU7, AU17, AU23) differed significantly from those with very high consistency (AU1, AU2, AU10, AU12, browsAU10; all ps < 0.05).

text.text: Thus, although landmark displacement varied in consistency across facial movements, it provided highly consistent motion estimates across avatars for most animations.

To evaluate whether landmark displacement was spatially concentrated in facial regions expected to move for a given AU, we computed the ratio of mean displacement in AU-relevant landmarks to mean displacement in all remaining landmarks (Figure 4D).
text.formatted: To evaluate whether landmark displacement was spatially concentrated in facial regions expected to move for a given AU, we computed the ratio of mean displacement in AU-relevant landmarks to mean displacement in all remaining landmarks (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4D</ref>).

text.text: Across animations, AU-relevant landmarks showed nearly twice as much displacement as the remaining landmarks (M = 1.94, SD = .70), with no significant differences across avatars (χ 2 (3) = 5.133, p = 0.162, Kendall's W = 0.095).
All animations yielded ratios above 1, indicating greater displacement in AU-relevant than in other facial landmarks.
However, the magnitude of this spatial correspondence varied significantly across animations (χ 2 (17) = 58.474, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.86).
text.formatted: However, the magnitude of this spatial correspondence varied significantly across animations (χ 2 (17) = 58.474, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.86).

text.text: The lowest ratios were observed for browsAll (M = 1.04, SD = 0.09), AU7 (lid tightener; M = 1.30, SD = 0.47), and AU6 (cheek raiser; M = 1.48, SD = 0.17).

In contrast, the highest ratios occurred for AU2 (outer brow raiser; M = 3.72, SD = 0.31), AU1 (inner brow raiser; M = 2.92, SD = 0.14), AU4 (brow lowerer; M = 2.72, SD = 0.11), and AU12 (lip corner puller; M = 2.51, SD = 0.3).

Together, these results show that landmark displacement provided highly consistent estimates of facial motion across avatars and that displacement was systematically concentrated in facial regions expected to move for the corresponding AUs.

Although both cross-avatar consistency and spatial correspondence still varied across facial movements, the findings demonstrate the potential of landmark displacement for characterizing facial motion independently of AU predictions.

In this study, we used controlled photorealistic facial animations with precisely specified motion to systematically evaluate methods for quantifying facial motion.

By applying identical facial rigging parameters across MetaHuman avatars, we could assess how reliably different methods captured known facial motion while varying the face on which that motion was expressed.

Our goals were threefold: first, to characterize the performance and potential biases of two widely used open-source AU-detection systems, OF and AFAR; second, to evaluate a complementary landmark-displacement approach that directly quantifies nonrigid facial motion from tracked geometry; and third, to provide FACET, an open-source toolbox that integrates both approaches within a unified and reproducible framework.

Across analyses, automated AU-detection systems performed above chance but varied substantially across facial movements and avatars, and neither system reliably recovered the temporal dynamics of the specified AU trajectories.

In contrast, landmark displacement yielded highly consistent motion estimates across avatars, with displacement systematically concentrated in facial regions expected to move for the corresponding AUs.

Together, these findings demonstrate the value of controlled stimuli with known motion parameters for evaluating facial motion quantification methods and highlight landmark displacement as a complementary approach for directly characterizing the geometric structure of facial motion.

By generating animations containing either isolated AUs or precisely controlled AU combinations, we could characterize systematic patterns in automated AU detection while knowing which facial movements were actually specified in each frame.
Across OF and AFAR, we identified several recurring limitations that help explain when and why automated AU estimates may deviate from the underlying facial motion.
Both systems showed an increased tendency to predict smile-related AUs (particularly AU12 and AU14).
These AUs were detected relatively well when present, but were also frequently predicted when absent, as reflected in their combination of high true-positive and false-positive rates.

This pattern is consistent with previous evaluations reporting systematic confusions among commonly co-occurring facial actions (Guo et al., 2018; Namba et al., 2021 Namba et al., , 2022;; Perusquia-Hernandez et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with previous evaluations reporting systematic confusions among commonly co-occurring facial actions <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Guo et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Namba et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Namba et al., , 2022;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Perusquia-Hernandez et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, Namba and colleagues (2021) found that both OF and AFAR overpredicted co-occurrence of AU14 with AU6, AU10, and AU12.

One possible explanation is that automated AU detectors partly learn the statistical cooccurrence structure of facial actions in their training data rather than relying exclusively on the local visual changes associated with individual AUs.
Previous work has shown that features informative for one AU can extend beyond its anatomically expected facial region.
For example, AU6 can be predicted from mouth-region information, likely reflecting its frequent co-occurrence with AU12 during smiling (Ertugrul et al., 2019b).
text.formatted: For example, AU6 can be predicted from mouth-region information, likely reflecting its frequent co-occurrence with AU12 during smiling <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Ertugrul et al., 2019b)</ref>.

text.text: Such learned dependencies may be beneficial for recognizing naturally occurring expressions, in which AUs frequently co-occur, but can lead to systematic false positives when individual facial actions are experimentally manipulated in isolation.
Our controlled animations make this distinction particularly apparent.
That is, because the underlying AU activations were precisely specified, predictions of non-activated AUs can be directly distinguished from genuine co-occurring facial motion.

For several AUs, including AU10, AU15, and AU23, both systems showed greater temporal correspondence with the ground-truth trajectories when these AUs occurred in combination with other facial movements than when they were presented in isolation.
Although perhaps counterintuitive, this finding is consistent with the co-occurrence effect described above.

Naturally occurring facial expressions typically comprise combinations of facial actions, and AU detectors trained on such data may therefore learn statistical dependencies between frequently co-occurring AUs.
As a consequence, an AU presented in a familiar combination may be easier to detect than the same movement presented in isolation.
Interestingly, this bias is in line with perceptual phenomena where humans perceive illusory slowing of feature motion when another facial feature is moving (Cook et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Interestingly, this bias is in line with perceptual phenomena where humans perceive illusory slowing of feature motion when another facial feature is moving <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Cook et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Our controlled animations provide a useful framework for investigating such dependencies because individual AUs and their combinations can be manipulated independently while keeping their activation trajectories precisely specified.

More broadly, synthetic facial animations could also be used to systematically vary AU co-occurrence during model training, providing a means to test whether more balanced exposure to isolated and combined facial actions improves the ability of AU-detection systems to recover individual facial movements.
We observed systematic differences across avatars, with both TPR and FPR higher for the two male avatars relative to the two female avatars.
Importantly, the simultaneous increase in true-and false-positive rates suggests a greater tendency to predict AU presence for these avatars rather than uniformly better detection performance.
Although this pattern could indicate gender-related differences, our sample of four avatars is too small to substantiate this interpretation.
Gender was also confounded with other factors (such as skin tone, facial structure, and textures) in our stimulus set.

Nevertheless, the finding that identical AU activation parameters produced different prediction patterns across avatars indicates that automated AU estimates depend not only on facial motion but also on the face on which that motion is expressed.
Such dependencies could potentially reflect biases in the demographic and visual composition of the datasets used to train AU-detection systems (Ertugrul et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Such dependencies could potentially reflect biases in the demographic and visual composition of the datasets used to train AU-detection systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Ertugrul et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Systematically varying individual facial characteristics while holding the underlying motion constant provides a promising approach for identifying the sources of these dependencies in future work.
Some AUs, particularly AU6 and AU7, and to a lesser extent AU23 and AU17, showed notably poorer performance.
Interestingly, AU6 and AU7 were also among the movements showing the lowest cross-avatar consistency and spatial correspondence in the landmarkdisplacement analysis.

One possible explanation is that these facial actions are expressed partly through local surface deformation, such as cheek raising, eyelid tightening, and changes in skin shape, which may not be fully captured by the displacement of a sparse set of facial landmarks.

Consistent with this possibility, previous work has highlighted the importance of appearance information for detecting facial actions whose expressions involve local changes in facial shape and texture (Namba et al., 2021; Zhi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Consistent with this possibility, previous work has highlighted the importance of appearance information for detecting facial actions whose expressions involve local changes in facial shape and texture <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Namba et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Zhi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, however, the limitations observed for AU detection cannot be attributed solely to landmark-based representations, as OF and AFAR incorporate additional visual information when predicting AUs.

The convergence across AU detection and landmark displacement instead suggests that some facial movements may be intrinsically more difficult to quantify from standard video-based representations than others, even under highly controlled viewing conditions.
Future work could test whether richer representations of facial surface deformation, including 3D mesh motion, depth or surface-normal information, improve the quantification of these movements.
The landmark-displacement analysis provided a complementary picture of facial motion to that obtained from automated AU detection.
Despite identical motion parameters across avatars, AU predictions varied systematically across faces and facial movements.
In contrast, landmark displacement patterns were highly consistent across avatars for most animations, and displacement was concentrated in facial regions expected to move for the corresponding AU.
An important distinction between the two approaches lies in what they aim to estimate.
an inference from the observed facial appearance and motion to an AU label.
This mapping can be influenced by statistical regularities in the training data, including AU co-occurrence, imbalanced AU frequencies, and variations in facial appearance.
Landmark displacement instead operates directly on tracked facial geometry, quantifying changes in landmark position without requiring these changes to be assigned to an AU category.
Our results show that this simpler representation can recover highly consistent patterns of geometric motion across different avatars when the underlying animation parameters are held constant.
This advantage comes with an important trade-off.
Landmark displacement describes the magnitude and spatial distribution of facial motion but does not provide the anatomical and semantic interpretation provided by FACS-based AU labels.
Moreover, because our implementation relies on automatically tracked landmarks, it remains dependent on the accuracy and potential biases of the underlying landmark detector.

Landmark displacement should therefore not be viewed as a replacement for AU detection, but as a complementary representation that is particularly useful when the primary question concerns the spatial and temporal structure of facial motion rather than its classification into predefined facial actions.
Our findings highlight the complementary information provided by different representations of facial motion.
Landmark displacement directly captures changes in facial geometry but may be less sensitive to facial actions expressed primarily through local surface deformation or appearance changes.

AU-detection systems can incorporate such appearance information, but introduce an additional inference step that may be influenced by learned co-occurrence statistics and variation in facial appearance.

Future approaches could therefore benefit from integrating multiple sources of information, including sparse or dense geometric motion, appearance, and 3D surface deformation, depending on the aspect of facial motion being quantified.
Controlled synthetic stimuli provide a useful framework for developing and evaluating such methods.
Facial actions can be manipulated independently, combined systematically, and reproduced across different faces while their underlying motion parameters remain known.

Beyond benchmarking existing methods, such stimuli could therefore be used to systematically manipulate AU co-occurrence and facial appearance during model development, helping to determine which representations and training distributions support more robust quantification of facial motion.

To facilitate the application and evaluation of facial motion quantification methods, we developed FACET, an open-source toolbox that integrates automated AU detection and landmark-based motion analysis within a unified framework.
By standardizing data processing and output formats across methods, FACET enables researchers to apply and compare different approaches within a reproducible workflow.

Combined with controlled facial animations with known motion parameters, it also provides a foundation for systematically evaluating existing methods and developing improved approaches to facial motion quantification.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the present findings.
First, our stimulus set comprised a small number of photorealistic adult MetaHuman avatars.

Although these avatars were selected to resemble identities commonly represented in existing AU-detection datasets, they do not capture the full diversity of facial morphology, age, or skin properties present in real-world populations.

Future work could systematically vary individual facial characteristics while holding motion constant to determine which aspects of facial appearance influence different facial motion quantification methods.
Second, the animations used here were intentionally short and highly controlled, with smooth, scripted motion trajectories designed to isolate specific facial actions.

While this level of control is essential for diagnostic model evaluation, it does not capture the temporal complexity of spontaneous facial behavior, including micro-expressions, asymmetric motion, speech-related dynamics, or context-dependent expressions.
Extending this approach to longer, more variable, and more naturalistic motion sequences would help determine how the observed patterns generalize beyond controlled facial animations.
Third, landmark displacement lacks the semantic interpretability inherent to FACSbased representations (Ekman et al., 2002) and depends on the accuracy of the underlying landmark tracker.
text.formatted: Third, landmark displacement lacks the semantic interpretability inherent to FACSbased representations <ref type="bibr">(Ekman et al., 2002)</ref> and depends on the accuracy of the underlying landmark tracker.

text.text: Future work should assess the robustness of this approach across different landmark detectors or explore denser representations, such as 3D facial meshes, to better capture local surface deformation.
Reliable quantification of facial motion is essential for studying how we perceive and understand dynamic faces.

By combining controlled photorealistic animations with AU-and landmark-based analyses, we show both the limitations of current AU-detection systems and the potential of landmark displacement as a complementary measure of facial motion.
With FACET, we provide an open and reproducible framework for quantifying facial motion in experimental data and systematically evaluating the methods used to capture it.
